icon: Users
description: Create accounts, open sessions, and sign users in with email, OAuth, magic links, MFA and more.

import { ShieldCheck, Users, Database, HardDrive } from 'lucide-react';

Applad authenticates end users per project. A user creates an **account**, opens
a **session**, and every request they make carries that session as a bearer
token. What they can then read or write is decided by their identity and the
[teams](/build/teams) they belong to (see [permissions](/build/permissions)).

This page covers the client-side account API: the endpoints your app calls on
behalf of the person using it. It runs under `/v1/account`. For creating and
managing users from your own backend (with an API key, no user session), see
[Server-side user management](#server-side-user-management) at the end.

![The console Auth tab listing a project's users](/screens/auth-users.png)
_Every account that signs into your app appears in the console's Auth tab, with its status and sessions._

## How a request authenticates

Every client request sends your project ID as a header:

```
x-applad-project: <projectId>
```

After a session is created, the request also carries the session's `secret` as a
bearer token:

```
Authorization: Bearer <secret>
```

The `secret` is a signed JWT returned once, in the body, when the session is
created. A browser also receives it as an `HttpOnly` cookie (`a_session_<projectId>`),
so a web app can rely on the cookie instead of storing the token in
JavaScript-readable storage. A mobile app or a script has no cookie jar, so it
keeps the `secret` and sends it as the header above.

Point an SDK client at your endpoint and project to begin:

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Dart']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```ts
import { Applad } from 'applad';

const client = new Applad({
  endpoint: 'https://api.applad.io',
  projectId: '<projectId>',
});
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Dart">
```dart
final client = Applad(
  endpoint: 'https://api.applad.io',
  projectId: '<projectId>',
);
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Create an account

Register a user with an email and password. `userId` defaults to a generated ID
(`unique()`); pass your own if you want to choose it. `name` is optional.

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Dart']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```ts
const user = await client.auth.createAccount('ada@example.com', 'super-secret', {
  name: 'Ada',
});
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Dart">
```dart
final user = await client.auth.createAccount(
  email: 'ada@example.com',
  password: 'super-secret',
  name: 'Ada',
);
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

Creating an account does not sign the user in. Open a session next.

The returned user object looks like this (`POST /v1/account`, `201`):

```json
{
  "$id": "a1b2c3...",
  "$createdAt": "2026-01-01T12:00:00Z",
  "$updatedAt": "2026-01-01T12:00:00Z",
  "name": "Ada",
  "email": "ada@example.com",
  "phone": "",
  "emailVerification": false,
  "phoneVerification": false,
  "status": true,
  "labels": [],
  "prefs": {}
}
```

<Callout title="Password length">
  Passwords must meet the project's minimum length (8 characters by default).
  A shorter password is rejected. A self-hoster can raise the minimum, and set
  a per-project user cap, in the project's auth security config.
</Callout>

## Email sessions

Sign a user in with their email and password. The response is a session whose
`secret` is the bearer token for everything that follows.

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Dart']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```ts
const session = await client.auth.createEmailSession('ada@example.com', 'super-secret');
client.setJWT(session.secret); // the JS SDK does not apply it for you

const me = await client.auth.getAccount();
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Dart">
```dart
final session = await client.auth.createEmailSession(
  email: 'ada@example.com',
  password: 'super-secret',
);
// The Dart SDK applies session['secret'] as the bearer token automatically.

final me = await client.auth.getAccount(); // already authenticated
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

<Callout title="The secret is what makes one session work everywhere">
  On the web, prefer the `HttpOnly` cookie the login also sets over keeping the
  secret in JavaScript. On mobile, persist the `secret` in secure storage
  (Keychain / Keystore) and restore it on the next launch. The Dart SDK applies
  the secret to subsequent requests for you; in the JS SDK, call
  `client.setJWT(session.secret)` yourself.
</Callout>

The session object (`POST /v1/account/sessions/email`, `201`):

```json
{
  "$id": "9f8e7d...",
  "$createdAt": "2026-01-01T12:05:00Z",
  "userId": "a1b2c3...",
  "expire": "2027-01-01T12:05:00Z",
  "provider": "email",
  "ip": "203.0.113.7",
  "userAgent": "Dart/3.3 (dart:io)",
  "current": true,
  "secret": "eyJhbGciOi..."
}
```

`secret` is present only on creation. Listing or fetching a session never returns
it.

<Callout title="When the account has MFA">
  If the user has enrolled a factor, email and password alone do not open a
  session: the endpoint returns `401` with type `user_mfa_required`. Resubmit
  the same `POST /v1/account/sessions/email` with a `code` field added, holding a
  TOTP or recovery code, and the session is issued on a valid code (an invalid
  one returns `401 user_mfa_invalid`).

  ```bash
  curl -X POST https://api.applad.io/v1/account/sessions/email \
    -H "x-applad-project: <projectId>" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"email": "ada@example.com", "password": "super-secret", "code": "123456"}'
  ```

  When the project sets `mfaRequired` but this user has no factor yet, the
  session opens normally and the `201` body adds `"mfaEnrollmentRequired": true`
  so you can route them into MFA setup. See
  [session and password security](#session-and-password-security) for the policy.
</Callout>

### Restoring a session on the next launch

Save the `secret` when you create the session, then restore it with `setJWT`
before making authenticated calls:

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Dart']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```ts
client.setJWT(savedSecret);
const me = await client.auth.getAccount();
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Dart">
```dart
// after reading the saved secret from secure storage
client.setJWT(savedSecret);
final me = await client.auth.getAccount(); // confirms it is still valid
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

By default a session lasts up to a year (a self-hoster can shorten this per
project). `getAccount` failing means the secret is expired or revoked; send the
user back to sign in.

## Anonymous sessions

Open a session with no account, so a user can start using your app before
signing up. Applad creates a throwaway user (labelled `anonymous`) and returns a
session exactly like an email session.

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Dart']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```ts
const session = await client.auth.createAnonymousSession();
client.setJWT(session.secret);
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Dart">
```dart
final session = await client.auth.createAnonymousSession();
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

The anonymous user is a real user row, so anything they create belongs to them.
To turn it into a permanent account later, set an email and password with the
account-update endpoints below while the anonymous session is still active.

## The current account

Every call below requires an active session.

### Read the account

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Dart']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```ts
const me = await client.auth.getAccount();
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Dart">
```dart
final me = await client.auth.getAccount();
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

### Update the name

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Dart']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```ts
await client.auth.updateName('Ada Lovelace');
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Dart">
```dart
await client.auth.updateName('Ada Lovelace');
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

### Update the email

Changing an email requires the current password.

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Dart']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```ts
await client.auth.updateEmail('ada@newmail.com', 'super-secret');
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Dart">
```dart
await client.auth.updateEmail(
  email: 'ada@newmail.com',
  password: 'super-secret',
);
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

### Update the password

Pass the old password to prove ownership. Changing the password invalidates the
user's other sessions by default, so they stay signed in only on the current
device.

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Dart']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```ts
await client.auth.updatePassword('a-new-secret', 'super-secret');
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Dart">
```dart
await client.auth.updatePassword(
  password: 'a-new-secret',
  oldPassword: 'super-secret',
);
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

### Preferences

Prefs are an arbitrary JSON object stored on the user, handy for per-user
settings. Updating replaces the whole object, so read, merge, then write if you
want to keep existing keys.

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Dart']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```ts
await client.auth.updatePrefs({ theme: 'dark', locale: 'en' });
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Dart">
```dart
await client.auth.updatePrefs({'theme': 'dark', 'locale': 'en'});
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

### Delete the account

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Dart']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```ts
await client.auth.deleteAccount();
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Dart">
```dart
await client.auth.deleteAccount();
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Managing sessions

A user can be signed in on several devices at once, each with its own session.

List every session for the current user (`GET /v1/account/sessions` returns
`{ total, sessions }`):

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Dart']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```ts
const { sessions } = await client.auth.listSessions();
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Dart">
```dart
final result = await client.auth.listSessions();
for (final s in result['sessions']) {
  print('${s['provider']} from ${s['ip']}, current: ${s['current']}');
}
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

Fetch one session, delete one session (sign out a single device), or delete all
of them (sign out everywhere):

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Dart']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```ts
await client.auth.getSession(sessionId);
await client.auth.deleteSession(sessionId);
await client.auth.deleteSessions();
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Dart">
```dart
await client.auth.getSession(sessionId);
await client.auth.deleteSession(sessionId); // one device
await client.auth.deleteSessions();          // everywhere; also clears the local token
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

<Callout title="Session limit">
  A user may hold up to 10 active sessions by default. When the limit is reached,
  creating a new session evicts the oldest one. Self-hosters can change this per
  project.
</Callout>

## Short-lived JWT

Ask Applad for a fresh JWT scoped to the current user, valid for 15 minutes. Use
it to authenticate the user to a service of your own, or to pass identity to
another system without handing over the long-lived session secret.

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Dart']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```ts
const jwt = await client.auth.getJWT();
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Dart">
```dart
final jwt = await client.auth.getJWT();
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

`POST /v1/account/jwt` returns `{ "jwt": "eyJ..." }`.

## OAuth2 sign-in

OAuth is a browser redirect flow, so it has no SDK method: you send the user to
an Applad URL, they authorise with the provider, and Applad redirects them back
with a session cookie set.

Start the flow by navigating the browser to:

```
GET /v1/account/sessions/oauth/{provider}?success=<path>&failure=<path>
```

`success` and `failure` are relative paths in your app that Applad redirects to
afterwards (absolute URLs are rejected to prevent open redirects). For example,
to sign in with Google:

```ts
const projectId = '<projectId>';
window.location.href =
  `https://api.applad.io/v1/account/sessions/oauth/google` +
  `?success=/dashboard&failure=/login`;
```

Applad handles the provider callback at
`/v1/account/sessions/oauth/{provider}/callback`, creates or links the user
(matching on the OAuth identity, then on the email), sets the session cookie, and
redirects to your `success` path.

<Callout title="OAuth sets a cookie, not a body token">
  The callback authenticates the browser by cookie and does not return the
  session `secret`. That makes it a good fit for web apps. For a native mobile
  OAuth flow you would capture the cookie or session yourself; the plain
  redirect flow documented here is browser-oriented.
</Callout>

### Available providers

A provider is active only when its credentials are configured. On a self-hosted
instance you enable one by setting `OAUTH_<PROVIDER>_CLIENT_ID` and
`OAUTH_<PROVIDER>_CLIENT_SECRET` (for example `OAUTH_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID`). Applad
defines these providers:

`google`, `github`, `apple`, `facebook`, `discord`, `twitter`, `microsoft`,
`slack`, `spotify`, `linkedin`, `gitlab`, `bitbucket`, `twitch`, `notion`,
`stripe`, `amazon`, `autodesk`, `bitly`, `box`, `dailymotion`, `disqus`,
`dropbox`, `etsy`, `figma`, `hubspot`, `kakao`, `line`, `mailchimp`, `patreon`,
`paypal`, `podio`, `reddit`, `salesforce`, `tradeshift`, `wordpress`, `yahoo`,
`yammer`, `yandex`, `zoho`, `zoom`.

Three more are configurable against your own identity provider and need a domain
or endpoints as well as credentials: `auth0` (`OAUTH_AUTH0_DOMAIN`), `okta`
(`OAUTH_OKTA_DOMAIN`), and a generic `oidc` (`OAUTH_OIDC_AUTH_URL`,
`OAUTH_OIDC_TOKEN_URL`, `OAUTH_OIDC_USERINFO_URL`).

You can also configure a provider per project from the console, under
Auth then Settings. Enter the client id and secret for a provider and enable it;
those credentials take precedence over the instance-wide `OAUTH_*` variables for
that project, so different apps on one instance can sign in through different
provider apps. The console never shows a stored secret back, and saving with the
secret field left blank keeps the one already stored. Providers configured this
way are managed through `GET`, `PUT`, and `DELETE`
`/v1/projects/{projectId}/auth/oauth`, which require a console session.

Some providers need more than a client id and secret, and the form collects
those fields too. Apple takes a Services ID, a Key ID, a Team ID, and the `.p8`
private key, from which Applad signs the short-lived ES256 client secret Apple
requires at each token exchange. Microsoft takes an optional Tenant ID that is
wired into the authorize and token endpoints, so a single-tenant Azure app works
instead of only the multi-tenant `common` endpoint. These auxiliary identifiers
are non-secret and may be read back to prefill the form; the client secret and
Apple's `.p8` key are secret, are stored encrypted at rest with
`CREDENTIALS_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, and are never returned.

## Multi-factor authentication (TOTP)

MFA uses time-based one-time passwords, the kind an authenticator app generates.
These endpoints require an active session and are not yet wrapped by the client
SDKs, so call them directly.

<Steps>
<Step>
### Enable MFA

Applad generates a TOTP secret and recovery codes, and returns an `otpauth://`
URI you can render as a QR code:

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.applad.io/v1/account/mfa \
  -H "x-applad-project: <projectId>" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <secret>"
```

```json
{
  "secret": "JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP",
  "recoveryCodes": ["01928374", "..."],
  "uri": "otpauth://totp/Applad?secret=JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP&issuer=Applad"
}
```
</Step>
<Step>
### Confirm a code

Confirm the user has added the secret to their authenticator by verifying a code.
MFA becomes enabled only after a code verifies:

```bash
curl -X PUT https://api.applad.io/v1/account/mfa \
  -H "x-applad-project: <projectId>" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <secret>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"code": "123456"}'
```
</Step>
</Steps>

Disable MFA (clears the secret and recovery codes):

```bash
curl -X DELETE https://api.applad.io/v1/account/mfa \
  -H "x-applad-project: <projectId>" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <secret>"
```

<Callout title="Sign-in challenges an enrolled factor">
  Once a user has enrolled a factor, the email-session endpoint challenges for
  it on every sign-in: a correct email and password alone returns
  `401 user_mfa_required` and no session. The client resubmits the same request
  with a `code` field holding a TOTP or recovery code, and only then is a
  session opened. Recovery codes are single-use, so store them safely. See
  "Email sessions" above for the request shape.
</Callout>

## Phone (SMS) sign-in

Sign a user in with a phone number and a one-time code sent by SMS, with no
password at all. Applad stores a short-lived code, texts it to the number, and
on a correct code opens a session. If no user has that phone number yet, one is
created (named `Phone User`). These endpoints have no client SDK method, so call
them directly.

<Callout title="Requires an SMS provider">
  The code is only texted when the instance has Twilio configured
  (`TWILIO_SID`, `TWILIO_TOKEN`, `TWILIO_FROM`). Without a provider the endpoint
  still records a code and returns `{"sent": true}`, but nothing is delivered, so
  phone sign-in is unusable until SMS is set up. See
  [Messaging](/build/messaging) for the provider settings.
</Callout>

<Steps>
<Step>
### Send the code

The phone number must be in E.164 format (a leading `+` and country code, for
example `+15551234567`); anything else is rejected. Applad generates a 6-digit
code that is valid for 10 minutes.

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.applad.io/v1/account/sessions/phone \
  -H "x-applad-project: <projectId>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"phone": "+15551234567"}'
```

The response echoes the number and never contains the code itself:

```json
{ "sent": true, "phone": "+15551234567" }
```
</Step>
<Step>
### Verify the code

Send the number back together with the code the user received. A correct,
unexpired code opens a session; the code is single-use and deleted on success.

```bash
curl -X PUT https://api.applad.io/v1/account/sessions/phone \
  -H "x-applad-project: <projectId>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"phone": "+15551234567", "code": "123456"}'
```

On success you get `201` with the session and its bearer token, and the browser
receives an `HttpOnly` `a_session` cookie:

```json
{
  "session": {
    "$id": "7c6b5a...",
    "userId": "a1b2c3...",
    "provider": "phone",
    "current": true
  },
  "token": "eyJhbGciOi..."
}
```

A wrong or expired code returns `401` with error code `auth_invalid_otp`. As
with email sessions, keep `token` and apply it with `setJWT` on a native client,
or rely on the cookie on the web.
</Step>
</Steps>

## Magic-link login

Send a one-time link that signs a user in without a password. If no account
exists for the email, one is created. These endpoints are not in the client
SDKs.

<Steps>
<Step>
### Request the link

`url` is your app's callback; Applad appends `?secret=<token>` to it and emails
the link (if SMTP is configured on the instance). The link expires in 15 minutes.

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.applad.io/v1/account/sessions/magic-link \
  -H "x-applad-project: <projectId>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email": "ada@example.com", "url": "https://yourapp.com/callback"}'
```
</Step>
<Step>
### Redeem the token

When the user lands on your callback, read `secret` from the query string and
redeem it to open a session:

```bash
curl -X PUT https://api.applad.io/v1/account/sessions/magic-link \
  -H "x-applad-project: <projectId>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"secret": "<token-from-the-link>"}'
```

Redeeming returns the session and sets the session cookie. It also marks the
email verified. The `secret` field is not included in the redeem response, so
this flow is browser-oriented, the same as OAuth.
</Step>
</Steps>

## Email verification

Verification confirms a user controls their email. It takes the user's ID, so
call it while they are signed in.

<Steps>
<Step>
### Send the verification email

The link expires in 24 hours:

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.applad.io/v1/account/verification \
  -H "x-applad-project: <projectId>" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <secret>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"userId": "<userId>", "url": "https://yourapp.com/verify"}'
```
</Step>
<Step>
### Confirm the token

Confirm the token from the emailed link:

```bash
curl -X PUT https://api.applad.io/v1/account/verification \
  -H "x-applad-project: <projectId>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"secret": "<token-from-the-link>"}'
```

On success the user's `emailVerification` flag becomes `true`.
</Step>
</Steps>

## Password recovery

Recovery lets a user who forgot their password set a new one over email.

<Steps>
<Step>
### Request the reset

Applad always responds `{"status": "sent"}`, whether or not the email exists, so
the endpoint never reveals which addresses have accounts. The link expires in one
hour.

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.applad.io/v1/account/recovery \
  -H "x-applad-project: <projectId>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email": "ada@example.com", "url": "https://yourapp.com/reset"}'
```
</Step>
<Step>
### Set the new password

Set the new password with the token from the link:

```bash
curl -X PUT https://api.applad.io/v1/account/recovery \
  -H "x-applad-project: <projectId>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"secret": "<token-from-the-link>", "password": "a-new-secret"}'
```
</Step>
</Steps>

## Session and password security

The defaults woven through the sections above (year-long sessions, up to 10 per
user, an 8-character password minimum) are a per-project policy an operator can
change. The policy lives in the project's `auth_config` under a `security` key,
and the management API exposes it on its own:

```
GET  /v1/projects/{projectId}/auth/security
PUT  /v1/projects/{projectId}/auth/security
```

`PUT` merges: it starts from the current settings and overlays the fields you
send, so you can change one value without restating the rest.

```bash
curl -X PUT https://api.applad.io/v1/projects/<projectId>/auth/security \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"passwordMinLength": 12, "sessionsPerUser": 5}'
```

The settings Applad enforces today:

| Field | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `passwordMinLength` | `8` | Shorter passwords are rejected on account creation and password reset with `password_too_short`. |
| `usersLimit` | `0` (unlimited) | Once the project holds this many users, new sign-ups fail with `users_limit_reached`. |
| `sessionsPerUser` | `10` | When a user is at the limit, opening a new session evicts their oldest one. `0` means unlimited. |
| `sessionLengthSeconds` | `31536000` (365 days) | How long a newly created session stays valid. |
| `invalidateOnPasswordChange` | `true` | Changing a password deletes the user's other sessions, leaving them signed in only on the current device. |
| `passwordPersonalData` | `false` | When on, a new password that contains the account email's local-part or a word from the user's name (case-insensitive, tokens of 3+ characters) is rejected with `password_personal_data`. Checked on sign-up, password change, and password recovery. |
| `passwordDictionary` | `false` | When on, a password whose exact value (case-insensitive) appears on Applad's built-in common/breached-password blocklist is rejected with `password_in_dictionary`. Checked on the same three paths. |
| `passwordHistory` | `0` (off) | When set to N, a password change or recovery that matches the current password or any of the last N is rejected with `password_reused`. Every successful password set is recorded (only the bcrypt hash) so the window builds forward from the moment the policy is switched on. |
| `sessionAlerts` | `false` | When on, a new password sign-in emails the user a "new sign-in" notice. It is skipped for the user's first session (the sign-in right after signup), for magic-link, email/phone OTP, and OAuth2 sign-ins, and when the account has no email on file. Requires email delivery to be configured; where none is, no alert is sent. |

<Callout title="How mfaRequired is enforced">
  `mfaRequired` is active policy, enforced without bricking existing accounts:

  - A user who has enrolled a factor is always challenged for a code at sign-in,
    whether or not the project sets `mfaRequired` (see "Multi-factor
    authentication" above).
  - When `mfaRequired` is on and a signing-in user has no factor yet, the
    session still opens (locking them out would strand every existing account),
    but the `201` response carries `"mfaEnrollmentRequired": true` alongside the
    usual session fields. Route that user into MFA setup, then require a factor
    on their next sign-in.

  The residual is deliberate: because enrolling a factor needs an active
  session, the server issues one rather than refusing it, so compelling
  enrolment is completed by the client acting on the flag. It cannot yet be
  enforced purely server-side for a user who ignores the signal. Every other
  field on this page is active policy.
</Callout>

## Server-side user management

The endpoints above act on the signed-in user. To manage users from your own
backend, use the server SDK with an API key (header `x-applad-key`), which reaches
`/v1/users`. There is no user session involved; the key authorises the whole
project.

```dart
// server SDK, authenticated with an API key
final user = await client.users.create(
  email: 'grace@example.com',
  name: 'Grace',
  password: 'temporary',
);

await client.users.list(search: 'grace', limit: 25);
await client.users.updateStatus(user['\$id'], false); // block a user
await client.users.deleteSessions(user['\$id']);       // force sign-out
```

Server-side you can also create users without a password (for invite flows),
update a user's email without their current password, and list or revoke any
user's sessions. Creating a user this way skips email verification.
